guide.title: South Williamsburg, Brooklyn: The South Side and Los Sures
guide.intro: The Village of Williamsburgh annexed part of the town of Bushwick in 1835 and split the new territory into three districts. The first of them was commonly called the South Side, and the name outlasted the village, the city and the annexation that followed. Sources generally place Division Avenue on the north of it, Broadway on the northeast, Flushing Avenue on the south and the East River on the west, though no single body sets an official boundary for any Brooklyn neighborhood. What the South Side became was decided after the Second World War, when two migrations arrived within a few years of each other and settled blocks apart: Hasidic refugees from Hungary and Romania, and Puerto Rican families drawn to work at the Brooklyn Navy Yard.

sections.heading: Two postwar arrivals
sections.body:
Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, arrived in New York from Europe on 27 September 1946, the second day of Rosh Hashanah, aboard the motor vessel Vulcania, and settled in Williamsburg with a small group of supporters. About eighteen months later, in late April 1948, his followers formally established Congregation Yetev Lev — the institutional foundation of the Satmar community now centered on South Williamsburg. Holocaust-survivor refugees, many of them Hasidic Jews from rural Hungary and Romania, had been arriving in Brooklyn during and after the war and concentrated in the area south of Division Avenue. A 2023 UJA-Federation study found the wider Williamsburg Jewish community numbers roughly 36,000 adults and 32,000 children in about 21,000 households, centered on Lee Avenue and Bedford Avenue south of Division Avenue.

Puerto Ricans began settling the Southside after the Second World War, drawn partly by the jobs at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, with Dominican migration following in the 1970s and 1980s. The neighborhood's Puerto Rican and Dominican residents and their advocacy organizations are known collectively as Los Sures, and Graham Avenue between Grand Street and Broadway is signed as the Avenue of Puerto Rico. El Puente, founded in 1982 by Luis Garden Acosta, Eugenio Maldonado and Dr. Frances Lucerna to address youth gang and street violence in Williamsburg and Greenpoint, still operates from 211 South 4th Street; it founded El Puente Academy for Peace and Justice in 1993, and Garden Acosta died in January 2019.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The neighborhood's subway service runs along Broadway, on the elevated BMT Jamaica Line, and the sources consulted describe these stations broadly rather than as South Williamsburg's own.

Marcy Avenue, at Marcy Avenue and Broadway, is served by the J at all times, the M at all times except late nights, and the Z in the rush-hour peak direction; its source describes the station as being in Williamsburg rather than specifically South Williamsburg. Hewes Street, at Hewes Street and Broadway, is served by the J at all times except the weekday peak direction and by the M at all times except late nights, and the Z skips it; its source likewise says Williamsburg. Flushing Avenue, at Flushing Avenue and Broadway on the neighborhood's stated southern boundary, is served by the same J and M pattern with the Z skipping it, and its source labels the station's neighborhood as Bedford-Stuyvesant while noting it also serves adjacent parts of Williamsburg and Bushwick.

The bus is a real answer here rather than a footnote. The B44 runs Lee Avenue southbound and Bedford Avenue northbound through the core of the neighborhood, stops at Hewes Street, and uses Roebling Street to reach its northbound terminus at the Williamsburg Bridge Plaza Bus Terminal. At Flushing Avenue, Lee Avenue becomes Nostrand Avenue.

On foot or by bicycle, the Williamsburg Bridge walkway leaves from the Broadway side of the neighborhood and crosses the East River to Manhattan's Lower East Side. It opened on April 23, 1904, closed for renovation in June 1991, and reopened in March 1992 rebuilt with 12-foot-wide pedestrian and bicycle paths.

faq.question: How do I get to South Williamsburg?
faq.answer: The J, M and Z serve the elevated Broadway stations at Marcy Avenue, Hewes Street and Flushing Avenue, though their sources describe them as Williamsburg and Bedford-Stuyvesant stations rather than South Williamsburg's own. The B44 runs Lee Avenue southbound and Bedford Avenue northbound through the core, and the Williamsburg Bridge walkway crosses to Manhattan from the Broadway side of the neighborhood.

faq.question: What does Los Sures mean?
faq.answer: It is the collective name for the neighborhood's Puerto Rican and Dominican residents and their advocacy organizations. Puerto Ricans settled the Southside after the Second World War, and Graham Avenue between Grand Street and Broadway is signed as the Avenue of Puerto Rico.

faq.question: Can visitors go inside the Satmar synagogues?
faq.answer: Assume not. Congregation Yetev Lev D'Satmar has synagogues on Rodney Street and at Kent Avenue and Hooper Street. These are active Hasidic houses of worship, and no source consulted for this guide states public visiting hours, tours, or open-to-the-public status for either building.

photos.title: Kings County Savings Bank at 135 Broadway
photos.description: The French Second Empire bank building of 1860-1867, a New York City landmark since 1966.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

places.name: Kings County Savings Bank Building
places.summary: A French Second Empire bank building on the Broadway boundary of the neighborhood, occupied by banks for over a century and by the Williamsburg Art & Historical Center since 1996. The center's own website reports the building has remained closed to the public since water damage in July 2025, so treat the exterior as the visit.
places.history: The building was constructed between 1860 and 1867 as the Kings County Savings Institution, designed by the architects Gamaliel King and William H. Willcox. It was designated a New York City individual landmark on March 15, 1966 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 16, 1980. The bank itself was liquidated on October 20, 1995.

places.name: Peter Luger Steak House
places.summary: A steakhouse at the Brooklyn foot of the Williamsburg Bridge, operating continuously under various ownership since 1887 and named to the James Beard Foundation's America's Classics list in 2002.
places.history: It opened in 1887 as Carl Luger's Cafe, Billiards and Bowling Alley in what was then a German neighborhood. After founder Peter Luger's death in 1941 the business declined under his son, until Sol Forman and Seymour Sloyer bought it at auction for $35,000 in 1950 and revived it. Descendants of the Forman and Sloyer families run it today.

places.name: Congregation Yetev Lev D'Satmar Synagogues
places.address: Rodney Street, and Kent Avenue at Hooper Street, Brooklyn
places.summary: Two large Hasidic synagogues of the Satmar community, one on Rodney Street and one at Kent Avenue and Hooper Street. They are active houses of worship; no source consulted for this guide addresses visitor access, and it should not be assumed.
places.history: The congregation was formally established in late April 1948 by the followers of Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, about eighteen months after he arrived in New York.

places.name: El Puente
places.summary: The headquarters of El Puente, a grassroots arts and social and environmental justice organization. It is a working community organization rather than a visitor attraction.
places.history: El Puente was founded in 1982 by Luis Garden Acosta, Eugenio Maldonado and Dr. Frances Lucerna to address youth gang and street violence in Williamsburg and Greenpoint. It founded El Puente Academy for Peace and Justice in 1993. Garden Acosta died in January 2019 and the organization continues operating.

entries.name: Kings County Savings Bank Building
entries.note: An 1860s bank on Broadway, landmarked in 1966. The arts center inside has been closed to the public since July 2025, so this is an exterior.

entries.name: Peter Luger Steak House
entries.note: Serving at the foot of the Williamsburg Bridge since 1887, when it opened as Carl Luger's Cafe, Billiards and Bowling Alley.

entries.note: Two Satmar synagogues, on Rodney Street and at Kent Avenue and Hooper Street. Active houses of worship, not visitor sites.

links.note: South Williamsburg and Greenpoint are both in Brooklyn Community District 1.
